name: Architectural Privacy Gradient

mechanism_chain.description: Walls, doors, screens, spatial depth, acoustic barriers, visual permeability create a gradient from public to intimate. Five levels: public → semi-public → semi-private → private → intimate.

data.finding: Privacy is a dual-channel phenomenon: visual exposure (% body visible from boundary) and acoustic exposure (STI)
data.effect: Architectural features directly determine privacy level

justification.backing: This is a constitutive relationship: the architectural features (wall opacity, aperture size, spatial depth, acoustic barriers) mathematically determine the visual and acoustic permeability that constitutes privacy.
justification.qualifier: Perceived privacy includes psychological factors beyond physical barriers (sense of control, familiarity, social context).
justification.rebuttal: Would fail if psychological factors dominate physical barriers; but evidence shows physical privacy correlates strongly with perceived privacy.

mechanism_chain.description: Altman's dynamic regulation model: individuals continuously adjust achieved privacy toward an optimum that varies by activity and state. Architectural features provide the adjustment mechanism — door closing, blind drawing, spatial retreat.

data.finding: Privacy is not a fixed need but a dynamic regulatory process; individuals continuously adjust achieved privacy toward an optimal point
data.effect: Architectural features serve as privacy adjustment mechanisms

justification.backing: Altman's privacy regulation theory holds that individuals have a dynamic optimal privacy level that varies with activity, mood, and social context. Architectural features (operable doors, screens, spatial options) are the primary regulatory mechanism.
justification.qualifier: The theory assumes occupants have access to privacy adjustment mechanisms. Fixed architectural features (no doors, no spatial options) prevent regulation.
justification.rebuttal: Would fail if privacy needs are fixed rather than dynamic; or if non-architectural mechanisms (social signals) dominate privacy regulation.

mechanism_chain.description: When achieved privacy < desired (unwanted intrusion): amygdala vigilance, RSA drop, behavioral withdrawal or territorial defense. When achieved privacy > desired (unwanted isolation): isolation biology onset per NM_SOCIAL_ISOLATION_ALLOSTATIC_001.

data.finding: Privacy violation produces immediate autonomic response: RSA drop, heart rate increase, skin conductance rise

justification.backing: Privacy violation in either direction (too little or too much) incurs autonomic cost. Intrusion triggers vigilance (amygdala-mediated); isolation triggers CTRA biology (see NM_SOCIAL_ISOLATION_ALLOSTATIC_001).
justification.qualifier: The bidirectional autonomic response is well-documented; the specific architectural-autonomic pathway involves inference from laboratory to field settings.
justification.rebuttal: Would fail if autonomic responses habituate rapidly to privacy mismatch; but evidence shows sustained mismatch produces chronic effects.

intimate.note: Requires solid boundary with operable closure

sharp_edge.description: Solid door, wall — binary privacy change

soft_edge.description: Progressive screening, spatial layering, gradual acoustic attenuation

regulation_effectiveness.note: Sharp edges provide more effective regulation but at cost of social connectivity

visual_complexity.description: Distance into a space from which an outsider can see occupants. Critical parameter for perceived privacy.

semi_private_STI.description: Speech audible but effortful to comprehend

ie_dpt_interaction: T_IE_002 (Privacy × Activity Demand) — the optimal privacy level is activity-contingent; a single privacy level for all activities is always suboptimal

sensory_sensitivity.note: Reduced tolerance for social unpredictability; need reliable privacy boundaries

anxiety_trait.note: Need visual escape route assessment; reject environments with only 'intimate' options (too enclosed)

age_group.note: May not use privacy regulation mechanisms effectively; environment should default to semi-private with easy social access

key_references: Altman, I. (1975). The Environment and Social Behavior. Brooks/Cole.
Gifford, R. (2014). Environmental Psychology: Principles and Practice (5th ed.). Optimal Books.

cross_template_interactions.IC2: Body Budget Prediction — privacy mismatch (too little or too much) incurs IC2 cost. Unwanted exposure produces vigilance-arousal cost; unwanted isolation produces social-deprivation cost. The optimal privacy gradient minimizes total IC2 expenditure across the activity cycle.
cross_template_interactions.AX4: Perceived Control — the critical feature is OPERABLE privacy boundaries. Fixed open-plan with no occupant-controllable privacy adjustment is a maximal AX4 violation. Operable doors, adjustable screens, and spatial choices restore AX4.
